idiom_name: function pointer plus void* context, invoked by the service
implementation_notes: C has no closures, so the classic structure is spelled out by hand: a function-pointer type carries the executable code and a void* argument carries the per-operation context, because the initiating stack frame is gone when the callback runs. The standard library demonstrates both halves - qsort takes only the comparator, while qsort_r adds an arg pointer precisely so the comparison function 'does not need to use global variables ... and is therefore reentrant and safe to use in threads'; pthread_create passes void* arg into the new thread the same way. The service stores the pair (a per-operation state machine, a registration table or a ring-buffer entry) and invokes the pointer from whichever thread or event loop owns the completion. Nothing replaces this structure in C: a callback interface cannot be expressed, so a vtable-shaped struct of function pointers is the only alternative when several entry points are needed.
pitfalls: A void* context that outlives its object (freed struct, closed descriptor, returned stack frame) turns the completion into a use-after-free; the callback must be detached before the context dies.

Calling back from a signal handler is limited to async-signal-safe functions because the handler runs on an arbitrary interrupted stack; anything else needs a deferred path such as a self-pipe or signalfd.
Nothing checks the function-pointer signature: casting an incompatible function or a mismatched context type compiles and corrupts the call.
Registrations are never removed automatically, so a stale function pointer left in a table is invoked later and crashes at an address that no longer means what it did.
